extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting press releases that follow the Associated Press (AP) Stylebook so releases are journalist-friendly, clear, and easily repurposed by media outlets. Covers punctuation, capitalization, numbers, formatting, structure, quotes, boilerplate and contact info.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AP style
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the press release in the style of the Associated Press using AP Stylebook rules for punctuation, grammar and formatting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following AP style makes releases more appealing and easier for journalists to use; it demonstrates professionalism, readability, consistency and efficiency. Use AP as the baseline for all punctuation, capitalization and formatting decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxford comma
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the Oxford (serial) comma in a simple series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'keynote speeches, panel discussions and networking opportunities' (no comma before 'and').

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a single space after a period (or other sentence-ending punctuation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use two spaces (a typewriter holdover). Apply one space after periods, question marks and exclamation points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double quotes for direct quotes and single quotes for quotes within quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place periods and commas inside quotation marks. Example: "This conference will be groundbreaking," Smith said.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas in dates
rubrics_metrics.description: When a month and year are mentioned without a specific date, do not use a comma; when a specific date is used, set off the year with commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example without day: 'June 2024.' Example with day: 'June 15, 2024.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphens and dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyphens to link words forming a single modifier before a noun and use an em dash with spaces on either side for emphasis or a change in thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example hyphen: 'cutting-edge technology.' Use spaced em dashes for breaks: word — word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline capitalization (title case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use title case for headlines and subheads: capitalize the first and last words and all major words; lowercase short articles, coordinating conjunctions and short prepositions unless first or last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'XYZ Corp Unveils New Tech at Annual Conference'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline length and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep headlines concise and descriptive; include the company name and the main news item; use strong active verbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a headline under 100 characters if possible; headlines 51–100 characters get the most views (per the cited report). Use present tense for immediate news and future tense for upcoming events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Dateline begins the first paragraph with the city in all capital letters followed by the date and an em dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For less-known cities include the state abbreviation. Examples: 'NEW YORK, June 15, 2023 –' or 'MANSFIELD, Mass., June 15, 2023 –'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductory paragraph (lead) — 5 Ws
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead (first paragraph) should summarize the entire news story and answer who, what, when, where and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the most newsworthy information first, write in active voice and use strong verbs. For events, include event name, host, date and location in the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body structure and information flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange the body in descending order of importance, expanding on details from the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short paragraphs (typically 2–3 sentences) to improve readability, especially on mobile. Intermix relevant quotes and keep the total release length around 300–500 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotes: attribution and first reference
rubrics_metrics.description: On first reference, give the person's full name and title; afterward use only the last name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Jane Smith, CEO of XYZ Corp.' then 'Smith said.' Capitalize formal titles when they appear before a name and lowercase them when they follow a name or are used alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotes: paragraphing and block quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Start a new paragraph for each new speaker; for quotes longer than three lines, use a block quote format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Block quotes should be indented for visual separation. Even if a quote continues the same subject, start a new paragraph for a different speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep periods and commas inside quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AP punctuation conventions for all quoted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate content and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a standardized company boilerplate at the end of the release with background information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the boilerplate to 100 words or less, include mission, founding date, main products/services and notable achievements; place it just before media contact information and keep it consistent across releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear media contact details for follow-up, including name, title, phone number and email address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example format: 'Media Contact: John Smith, PR Manager, XYZ Corp, 555-123-4567, [email protected]'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of job titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize formal titles when they appear before a name; lowercase them when they follow the name or appear alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'CEO Jane Smith announced...' but 'Jane Smith, chief executive officer, announced...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company and product name stylization
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect the company's or product's official capitalization and stylization, even if unconventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proper noun starts with a lowercase letter (e.g., 'iPhone'), capitalize it at the beginning of a sentence. When unsure, verify the official styling (e.g., via a web search).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers: general rules and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out numbers one through nine; use numerals for 10 and above. Use numerals for ages, percentages, dimensions, temperatures, times, dates, monetary amounts and sports scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out numbers at the beginning of a sentence (except years). Ordinals: spell out first through ninth, use numerals for 10th and above. For very large numbers, use a combination of numerals and words (e.g., '1.5 million').

rubrics_metrics.name: Fonts, sizes and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Use common readable fonts and keep font sizing consistent; emphasize sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended fonts: Times New Roman, Arial or Calibri. Body text: 10–12 points; headlines: typically 14–16 points. Do not mix multiple fonts or sizes; avoid underlining (it can be confused with hyperlinks). Use bold or italics sparingly for emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active voice and strong verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor active voice and strong, specific verbs throughout the release to create impact and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the lead and headlines use active constructions and verbs like 'launches', 'announces', 'hosts' rather than passive phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length guideline for press release
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for a concise overall length for readability and journalist adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target 300–500 words total, long enough to include essentials but concise enough to retain attention.
